newsitem.title: UK: International LPG quiet in Asia as Japan holds bac.
newsitem.headline: International LPG quiet in Asia as Japan holds bac.

text.p: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) markets were subdued this week in the east of Suez markets as players remained uncertain of Saudi Aramco's acceptances for the May loading programme, and Japanese and South Korean buyers were still holding back from trading, dealers said.
There was better interest in Europe, with material moving from the Mediterranean to the North Sea as well as in the reverse direction.

"Before Saudi Aramco's acceptances are known, nobody is moving, especially buyers," said a trader concentrating on the East Asian market. He added that price discussion against the May Saudi Contract Price (CP) - the benchmark at which most LPG east of Suez is traded - is now at around May CP -$15/-$10 a tonne for propane and CP -$5 a tonne for butane, both on a fob Gulf basis.

Many are expecting the May CP to be set at between $173 and $175 a tonne for propane and around $185 to $187 a tonne for butane. This is based on an award for the T1 tender, the first of Aramco's three monthly spot tenders which contribute to the CP, said to be at $165 a tonne for propane and $180 a tonne for butane.
The T2 tender closes on Friday, and a trader said it was expected to be awarded at a lower level.
Against the April CP, propane is assessed by traders at CP -$30/-$25, while butane is seen at CP -$25/-$15, but trade was thin.
"There's no interest at all for either product in Japan," said a Japanese trader. "The CP is still very high and people are thinking that in one or two months it will be much lower."

The same situation applies to South Korea, where spot buyers are still holding off waiting for lower prices, although in China there are fewer availabilities on offer and prices are firming slightly to over CP +$50 a tonne C+F South China, a dealer said.
Japanese C+F prices are notionally $20 a tonne above the fob Gulf price, representing the freight cost for the journey.

In Europe, the price level in the north was set early in the week when a 40,000 tonne cargo of Algerian propane for second half April delivery traded at a private and confidential price between $175 and $180 a tonne cif Terneuzen.
Although neither side would confirm the details, some put the price at $176 or $177 cif. Dealers said this price was still valid by the end of the week.

Even though this cargo had moved from Algeria to ARA, the Mediterranean price was stronger although demand was not so great. The same seller sold a 20,000 tonne cargo in the high 190's cif Lavera/Livorno for 2-port discharge in the middle of the week.

One trader said a major had sold part of a North Sea cargo to a French affiliate at around $185 cif Lavera after the large 20,000 tonne deal, so that product moved both North to South and South to North in the same week.

The main European demand for butane was seen coming from Turkey. A Scandinavian producer reported buying a 6,000 tonne lot of refinery butane from the UK at $158 a tonne fob UK South Coast, which will be added to another lot to make up a 30,000 tonne cargo for Turkey.
Another dealer said most Mediterranean demand for butane was coming from Turkey, accounting for its value at a premium of around $5 a tonne to propane.

In the US, LPG levels slipped on Thursday following the release of Energy Information Administration data showing a build-up of propane stocks by 1.5 million barrels to 26.7 million barrels, the highest at this time of year since 1992. Both propane and butane fell on the news, although propane later recovered in line with crude prices to a little over 34 cents a gallon at Mont Belvieu, while butane continued to fall to 37.50/38 cents a gallon at Mont Belvieu.
